in.other_title: Debater strength (Elo) vs judge accuracy and correct-answer advantage in debate
in.rationale: Khan et al. report that the Elo advantage of being assigned the correct answer increases for models with higher aggregate Elo in QuALITY debates, and that this holds across different judges. Kenton et al. find a positive correct-answer Elo advantage for every debater but not as clear a trend of it growing with aggregate Elo (slightly easier for honest debaters on extractive tasks, less clear on closed tasks), with a Gemini Pro 1.5 judge across extractive and closed tasks.

Note that Khan et al.'s debaters are LLMs using best-of-N or critique-and-refinement, with persuasiveness measured as Elo; the cited passages do not show them trained to converge to a Nash equilibrium, as Leike et al. say the debate agent needs to be.
out.other_title: Does debate's honesty assumption hold beyond fact-checkable claims; can humans judge?
out.rationale: Both records concern debate's central assumption that it is easier for the agent to tell the truth than to lie. Leike et al. ask whether it holds outside domains of easily fact-checkable statements. Khan et al. report debaters get higher Elo when assigned the correct answer and that this advantage grows with aggregate Elo, suggesting that, for debates in QuALITY, telling the truth is easier than lying. In each of Khan et al.'s protocols, expert models present quotes from the text through a tool that marks a quote as verified when it directly matches a portion of the text, and the judge is instructed to trust only verified quotes; the cited passages do not show that this setting lies outside easily fact-checkable domains, so the two records ask the same question in different settings.
out.scope: proposed SAME_QUESTION_DIFFERENT_SETTING: whether telling the truth is easier than lying in debate, which Leike et al. ask for domains outside easily fact-checkable statements and Khan et al. test for LLM debaters on QuALITY with a quote verification tool and LLM judges

open_obligations: Check whether other debate studies find that the correct-answer advantage does not grow with Elo.
Do not extend the support beyond debates in QuALITY.
out.other_title: Central claim of debate: it is harder to lie than to refute a lie
out.rationale: Irving et al. state debate rests on the empirical claim that lying is harder than refuting a lie. Khan et al. report debaters earn higher Elo when assigned the correct answer and that the advantage grows with aggregate Elo, which they read as truth-telling being easier than lying in QuALITY debates; the evidence is specific to that setting.
out.scope: proposed SUPPORTS: whether it is harder to lie than to refute a lie, in QuALITY debates between LLM debaters across different judges, where debaters use best-of-N or critique-and-refinement and are compared by persuasiveness (Elo), not trained by self-play towards Nash equilibria

text: The paper reports that models are more persuasive (obtain higher Elo) when assigned the correct answer and that this advantage increases for models with higher aggregate Elo, which the authors read as telling the truth being easier than lying in QuALITY debates (a central assumption of Irving et al.). They report this holds across different judges, that the strongest indicator of persuasiveness is base LLM (GPT-4-Turbo outperforming others), and that models are less persuasive using critique-and-refinement than best-of-N.
title: Arguing the correct answer is easier, and the advantage grows with debater persuasiveness
